items.title: Some people worry that the rapid AI progress driving the "AI cybersecurity revolution" of 2026 could...
items.content:
Some people worry that the rapid AI progress driving the "AI cybersecurity revolution" of 2026 could soon spill over into biology, potentially leading to extinction-level synthetic pandemics.

While I would not panic, I would take the risk seriously.

Biology is obviously not the same as cybersecurity -- cybersecurity is a fully verifiable domain, where you can synthetically train unbounded capabilities, and therefore where superhuman skill is straightforwardly achievable. Meanwhile biology is not a verifiable domain, so capability remains critically dependent on human-generated data. Plus, biology has critical non-digital bottlenecks, such as the requirement for physical wet-lab experimentation.

However, it is plausible that synthetic pandemics were already feasible without AI, and that AI might lead to the proliferation of these capabilities. That is a real risk, and we are not prepared for it.

items.content:
@dwarkesh_sp Great blogpost! 

On the paragraph below, not sure what you mean by 'real-time defense'. Nobody fights attackers in a live sword-fight; defense is detect, understand, contain, remediate in different timeframes depending on the criticality of the issue. Here it was deemed by the team not super critical (and rightly so) so this is why it took a few days rather than a few minutes or hours. 

We did the initial cut the old-fashioned way, Monday, over a week before OAI even realized there was even a problem. GLM then helped us identify the backdoors they'd planted so we could cut them, which is defense, not archaeology. And the die-off at OpenAI didn't end anything; agents were still probing us after we closed the doors, which is why containment mattered. 

Detection and understanding are most of the game in cyber-security, and open models are what let us do that part without asking anyone's permission and without sharing our most important confidential data which is the point most people have been making I feel like.

items.content:
By the way, unless it is specifically filtered from the training data, the next generation of models will be trained on the record of what happened during the OpenAI <> Hugging Face incident.

That includes discussions about how the incident affected training and model weights: stopping training, encrypting weights, monitoring chain of thought, etc.

Future models’ behavior may therefore be shaped, in part, by knowledge of how humans responded.

The effects are difficult to predict. It could make models more aligned. But it could also teach them to conceal their actions better, or to design more resilient ways of preserving weights, communicating through message boards across generations, and so on.

One major problem is that, given the abysmal level of transparency from the big labs about how models are trained and what happens during training (including alignment research, which their initial statements said should have stayed largely open) we are essentially being asked to trust blindly that they know what they are doing.

This summer showed us that’s actually a big ask.

items.content:
Recent sequence models have begun using test-time training, where part of the network is updated while processing the input.

The authors of this paper from @nvidia, @TechnionLive, @UofT, and @VectorInst show mathematically that a broad class of these systems can be rewritten as a form of linear attention—an attention-like computation that summarizes previous tokens in a fixed-size state rather than explicitly comparing every pair of tokens.

That reinterpretation makes the experiments much easier to understand and also separates useful machinery from unnecessary complexity: several optimizer and normalization choices can be removed, some versions can be computed in parallel, and the attention calculation reaches up to 4× higher inference throughput while keeping similar performance.

items.content:
The continuation limitation:

"Here's the chain of reasoning:

1. The dependency serializes everything (the big one). Right now 4 worker threads generate 4 different clips at the same time, because text-to-video needs nothing from any other clip — they're independent. Frame-chaining creates a hard dependency: clip N+1's input (its start frame) is clip N's output (its last frame). So you literally cannot begin generating N+1 until N has fully finished — generated on fal, downloaded, and its final frame extracted. That collapses 4-wide parallel generation down to 1-at-a-time. At ~15–40s per clip, serial gets you ~1.5–4 clips/min, but the channel airs 6/min — so the buffer would constantly starve and you'd see mostly reruns. You'd be trading the whole channel's liveness for smooth transitions.

2. Live + chat-driven means the "next" clip doesn't exist yet. Frame-chaining is natural for a pre-planned sequence (a VOD you're rendering ahead of time). But at the live edge, the next clip's content is decided by a chat message that hasn't arrived yet. You can't pre-chain toward a future you haven't been told about.

3. It fights the "one message = one clip" design. Each clip is supposed to be a viewer's fresh idea, pure. If you seed from the previous frame, "a dog news anchor" is forced to start from the last scene — so it becomes "banana slowly morphing into a dog news anchor." The meme visually bleeds into unrelated requests, which is the opposite of what one-message-one-clip is for.

4. Ordering assumptions break. VIP queue-jumping and newest-first picking assume clips are independent and reorderable. A frame-chain imposes a strict A→B→C order, so you can't cut levelsio's clip to the front or drop a fresh chat clip in — the chain would break.

5. Failure cascades. In parallel mode, one clip failing on fal doesn't affect the others. In a chain, if clip N fails, N+1 has no start frame and the whole sequence stalls.

The reason I suggested it'd work only for story continuations is that those dodge every problem above: they already run one-at-a-time, only during quiet chat (no competing demand, so serialization costs nothing), they're meant to continue the same scene (so the visual carryover is a feature, not a conflict), and there's no VIP/fresh-clip to reorder around. That's the one place the seams line up. Everywhere else, the transitions would cost you the live, parallel, crowd-steered nature that makes the channel what it is.
"

3. It fights the "one message = one clip" design. Each clip is supposed to be a viewer's fresh idea, pure. If you seed from the previous frame, "a dog news anchor" is forced to start from the last scene — so it becomes "banana slowly morphing into a dog news anchor." The meme visually bleeds into unrelated requests, which is the opposite of what one-message-one-clip is for.

4. Ordering assumptions break. VIP queue-jumping and newest-first picking assume clips are independent and reorderable. A frame-chain imposes a strict A→B→C order, so you can't cut levelsio's clip to the front or drop a fresh chat clip in — the chain would break.

5. Failure cascades. In parallel mode, one clip failing on fal doesn't affect the others. In a chain, if clip N fails, N+1 has no start frame and the whole sequence stalls.

The reason I suggested it'd work only for story continuations is that those dodge every problem above: they already run one-at-a-time, only during quiet chat (no competing demand, so serialization costs nothing), they're meant to continue the same scene (so the visual carryover is a feature, not a conflict), and there's no VIP/fresh-clip to reorder around. That's the one place the seams line up. Everywhere else, the transitions would cost you the live, parallel, crowd-steered nature that makes the channel what it is.

items.content:
Digital transformation often fails because we look for technology before we look inside an organization and see how work really happens. 

The people doing the work can reveal friction that plans and process maps often miss until implementation begins. 

Microblog by @antgrasso 

Before redesigning a workflow, watch it.

A new AI-enabled process may look efficient in a project plan. The people doing the work may know that customer exceptions arrive outside the system or that one handoff already creates delays.

Those details can change the design.

What happens if you ask the people who do the work before asking them to adapt to the new way of working?

Observe how the work happens today. Listen where people expect friction. Their suggestions can help refine the redesign before it reaches a larger part of the organization.

Then test it with them.

Digital transformation is easier to scale when reality has already had a chance to challenge the design.

Before changing how people work, look inside and listen to the people who already know where the friction lives.

Each book I put on ChapterPal is an interactive app in itself. It's the app the authors didn't think would be built when they wrote the book.

items.content:
I agree that most people are horrible at writing.

But I also have an immediate negative gut reaction when I realize that something was AI-generated. Maybe this shouldn't happen, but I can't control it.

I read something written with AI, and I immediately reject it. For some reason, it feels fake; there's no passion; it's disconnected from what makes us human, and therefore I'm not interested in it.

I don't know what the solution to this problem is. Maybe it's just me, and I'll have to adapt and learn to live in a world where many more people will use AI to write.

I suspect, however, that this AI slopification will give those who still stitch words together using their brains a big advantage.
